intro.title: What is serv_aligner?
intro.md:
`serv_aligner` is the **instruction fetch aligner** of the SERV RISC-V CPU, and at 67 lines it is the smallest module in the design. That makes it the perfect first conversion to study.

**The problem it solves:** when SERV runs *compressed* (16-bit) instructions, the program counter can land in the **middle** of a 32-bit memory word. But memory only returns whole aligned words. So the aligner plays a small trick with two registers:

- `lower_hw` (16 bits) remembers the **upper half** of the word fetched last time
- `ctrl_misal` (1 bit) remembers "we are currently misaligned"

When misaligned, it fetches the *next* word (`address + 4`) and glues the two halves together: `{new_word[15:0], lower_hw}`. It also uses `ack_en` to hide the first memory acknowledge from the CPU, because a misaligned fetch secretly needs **two** bus transactions.

**The journey you are about to replay:** an AI agent converted this Verilog to TL-Verilog in 15 small steps. Every step had to pass **FEV** (Formal Equivalence Verification), a mathematical proof that the change did not alter the circuit's behavior. Use **Next** to walk forward, watch the editor for what changed, and hit **▶ Run check** to see the verification verdict.

1.title: Build the safety net first
1.md:
Notice the editor shows **zero code changes**. A conversion never starts by editing code. It starts by building the scaffolding that makes every later edit provable:

- the original Verilog was copied to `prepared.sv` (the frozen reference), `wip.tlv` (the file the AI will edit), and `feved.tlv` (the last version that passed verification)
- `fev.eqy` and `fev_full.eqy` were created: the configs that tell the EQY prover **which two files to compare**
- `tracker.md` and `status.json` were created for notes and progress

Then `fev.sh` ran once on two *identical* files. Why bother? To prove the verification pipeline itself works before any real change. If this fails, something is wrong with the tools, not the code.

**Try it:** open *Files at this checkpoint* and peek at `fev.eqy`.

2.title: Tell the prover which signals match
2.md:
Still no code changes, but open `fev_full.eqy` in *Files* and you will see new `gold-match` lines for every internal signal:

```
gold-match ibus_rdt_concat ibus_rdt_concat
gold-match ack_en ack_en
gold-match lower_hw lower_hw
gold-match ctrl_misal ctrl_misal
```

**Why this matters more than it looks:** EQY does not compare two circuits in one giant proof. It cuts them into small partitions at *matching signals* and proves each piece separately. This flow does **not** use reset to synchronize the two circuits, so every register (`lower_hw`, `ctrl_misal`) **must** be matched, otherwise the prover assumes they can start with different values and the proof fails.

This is the #1 source of FEV failures in the whole project: rename a signal, forget to update the match list, watch the proof break.

3.title: Check for parameters (there are none)
3.md:
The AI inspected the module for Verilog `parameter`s and `generate` blocks. Parameterized modules must be proven for **several parameter values** (each gets its own `fev_full_*.eqy` config), because logic that is correct for `W=1` can be broken for `W=4`.

`serv_aligner` has no parameters and no generate blocks, so nothing to do. Compare with `serv_alu`, which needed a separate `fev_full_W_4.eqy`.

A do-nothing step still gets a checkpoint: that is what makes the history a complete, replayable record.

4.title: Audit the clock and reset
4.md:
TL-Verilog has two hard requirements before any conversion can start:

1. one free-running clock named exactly `clk`
2. a **synchronous** reset (TL-Verilog cannot express asynchronous reset)

The AI audited the code: the clock is already `clk` ✓, and `rst` is read inside `always @(posedge clk)`, never in the sensitivity list, so it is synchronous and positively asserted ✓. No edits needed.

**One honest detail:** the status recorded at this snapshot says `3: Incremental FEV failed`. That is a leftover from a *failed attempt* during this task, before this passing checkpoint was saved. The history keeps that trace, which is exactly the kind of breadcrumb you want when debugging an agent.

5.title: Wrap the Verilog in a TL-Verilog shell
5.md:
The first real edit, and it is a big one (62 lines), yet **behavior changes zero**. The file becomes a TL-Verilog file with the Verilog tucked inside:

```
\TLV_version 1d: tl-x.org
\SV
module serv_aligner (...);
\TLV
   |default
      @0
         \SV_plus
            ...all the original logic...
\SV
endmodule
```

Read the new scaffolding from outside in:

- `\SV` regions hold plain SystemVerilog (the module ports)
- `\TLV` is where TL-Verilog lives
- `|default` declares a pipeline, `@0` declares stage 0 of it
- `\SV_plus` is a **Verilog island inside TL-Verilog**: original code can sit here unchanged until it is ready to migrate

Also note everything is re-indented to exactly 3 spaces per level. In TL-Verilog, indentation IS structure, like Python.

6.title: One tiny rename: rst becomes reset
6.md:
A deliberately tiny step: create `wire reset = rst;` and use it in place of `rst`.

Why bother? TL-Verilog's conventions expect a positively-asserted reset called `reset`, and later steps will turn it into the pipesignal `$reset`. Renaming **now**, while the code is still plain Verilog, keeps the later (riskier) steps smaller.

This is the agent's core discipline you will see again and again: *make the smallest change that FEV can verify, then checkpoint*. Seven changed lines, one new wire, proof, done.

7.title: Signals become pipesignals ($)
7.md:
The signature TL-Verilog concept arrives. Every internal signal gets a `$` and stops being declared:

```
assign $$ack_en = ! (i_ibus_adr[1] & ! $ctrl_misal);
```

Two new spellings to learn:

- `$$name[range]`: "this Verilog statement **assigns** pipesignal `$name`". Inside an `\SV_plus` island, SandPiper does not parse the Verilog, so the `$$` marks the assignment explicitly, with its bit range
- `$name`: an ordinary **use** of the pipesignal

The `wire`/`reg` declarations are deleted because TL-Verilog declares a signal by assigning it.

**Now open *Files* → `fev.eqy`.** Because every signal changed its generated Verilog name, the match list had to follow:

```
gold-match lower_hw |default<>0$lower_hw
```

That line says: old signal `lower_hw` = pipesignal `$lower_hw` in stage 0 of pipeline `|default`. Rename without updating this list and FEV fails, which is exactly the bug Arya hit on serv_decode.

8.title: Sweep up the leftover declarations
8.md:
The previous step converted assignments; this one deletes the now-orphaned `reg [15:0] lower_hw;` and `reg ctrl_misal;` declarations (3 lines).

The task is named *Non-vector Signals* because its real job is hunting for signals with types TL-Verilog cannot express directly (structs, signed values). `serv_aligner` has none, so the step degenerates into housekeeping.

Small lesson hiding here: the registers did not disappear, they are still inferred by the `$$lower_hw <= ...` flop assignment. Only the *declarations* became redundant.

9.title: if/else becomes ternary, hidden state becomes visible
9.md:
TL-Verilog wants each signal assigned by **one expression**, so the two `always`-block conditionals get rewritten:

```
$$lower_hw[15:0] <= i_wb_ibus_ack ? i_wb_ibus_rdt[31:16] : $lower_hw;

$$ctrl_misal <= $reset ? 1'b0 :
               (i_wb_ibus_ack & i_ibus_adr[1]) ? ! $ctrl_misal :
               $ctrl_misal;
```

Look closely at the last line of each ternary: `: $lower_hw` and `: $ctrl_misal`. The original Verilog had `if (ack) lower_hw <= ...` with **no else**, which silently means "otherwise keep the old value". The ternary is forced to say that out loud: *recirculate yourself*.

This explicitness is the point: hidden hold-state is where Verilog bugs live, and TL-Verilog refuses to hide it.

10.title: Leave the island: logic becomes native TL-Verilog
10.md:
The biggest conceptual jump in the whole conversion. The logic walks out of the `\SV_plus` island and becomes real TL-Verilog expressions:

```
<<1$lower_hw[15:0] = *i_wb_ibus_ack ? *i_wb_ibus_rdt[31:16] : $lower_hw;
```

Three things changed at once:

- **`<<1$lower_hw = ...`** assigns the value `$lower_hw` will have **one cycle in the future**. That is the whole flip-flop: no `always @(posedge clk)`, no `<=`. A register is now just an equation about time
- **`*i_wb_ibus_ack`**: the `*` prefix marks a raw Verilog signal (the module ports) referenced from TL-Verilog context
- `assign` keywords are gone: TL-Verilog statements are declarative

Compare the editor's red lines (Verilog always-blocks) with the green lines replacing them. Same circuit, FEV-proven, but the *clock has disappeared from the source code*. SandPiper puts it back when generating Verilog.

11.title: Push Verilog to the edges

12.title: Tidy: make it read like the original
12.md:
Pure cleanup, formally proven harmless:

- the temporary `$rst` hop is gone: `$reset = *rst;` directly
- the original designer's comments (the big *From SERV core to Memory* block) move back next to the logic they describe

This reflects a project rule that is easy to underestimate: the converted file should *look like the original file*, same comments, same order, same story. The goal of the whole project is maintainable code that humans recognize, not machine output that happens to be equivalent.

13.title: Switch on the M5 preprocessor
13.md:
Three lines:

```
\m5_TLV_version 1d: tl-x.org
\m5
   use(m5-1.0)
```

M5 is TL-Verilog's macro preprocessor (think of it as a much smarter `#define`). Nothing uses it *yet*: this step exists only so the **next** step can define a reusable macro.

Note the agent's discipline again: enabling a preprocessor and using a preprocessor are two separate, separately-verified steps. If FEV broke, you would know exactly which of the two ideas broke it.

14.title: The payoff: a reusable component
14.md:
The finale. The core logic is lifted into a named TL-Verilog macro:

```
\TLV serv_aligner_logic(/_top)
   |default
      @0
         <<1$lower_hw[15:0] = ...
         $ibus_rdt_concat[31:0] = ...
         $ack_en = ...
         <<1$ctrl_misal = ...
```

and the module body shrinks to: bind inputs → `m5+serv_aligner_logic(/top)` → drive outputs.

Step back and look at what 67 lines of Verilog became: **four equations**. And the same file now works two ways: instantiate it as a normal Verilog module, or drop `m5+serv_aligner_logic(...)` straight into any other TL-Verilog design as a library component. This dual-use structure is the template every other SERV module follows.

15.title: The end-to-end proof
15.md:
No code changes. The final `fev.sh` run proves the finished `wip.tlv` equivalent to the **original** `prepared.sv` across the *entire* conversion, not just step-to-step. That single proof is what lets you trust 14 steps of AI edits without reading any of them.

The AI also finalized its report: open **Conversion report** in the left panel to read the handoff summary (original 68 lines → 65 lines of TL-Verilog, core logic 15 lines, zero outstanding issues).

**Where to go from here:** you just watched the recipe that every conversion follows. The next module up in difficulty is `serv_mem_if`, then `serv_alu` with its `W=1`/`W=4` parameter twist, the exact thing step 3 got to skip.
